title: Editors
lead: Edit text files in the terminal: nano for a quick start, vi/vim when it has to be everywhere and fast.
objectives: You open, edit, save and close files with nano.
You know vim's modes and can always get out of vim (:q!, :wq).
You use basic vim commands: insert, delete a line, undo, search.
You edit config files safely: backup first, sudo only when needed.

sections.title: nano: the easy editor
body: `nano` is beginner friendly: you start typing right away and the shortcuts are listed at the bottom of the screen. `^` means the **Ctrl** key, so `^X` is Ctrl+X.

If the file does not exist, `nano file` opens an empty buffer and creates the file when you save. On Ubuntu nano is usually preinstalled; on Rocky/Alma install it with `sudo dnf install nano` if needed.

commands.what: Opens a file in the nano editor (creates it on save if missing).
commands.where: For quick edits of text and config files.
commands.why: Simple, with visible help at the bottom.

commands.what: Writes out (saves) the file; confirm the name with ENTER.
commands.where: Inside nano, whenever you want to save.
commands.why: Saves your work without leaving the editor.

commands.what: Exits nano; asks to save if there are unsaved changes (Y/N).
commands.where: Inside nano, when you are done.
commands.why: The way out: Y saves, N discards.

commands.what: Cuts the current line / pastes it back.
commands.where: To delete, move or duplicate lines.
commands.why: Fast line editing without a mouse.

sections.tip: More nano keys: `Ctrl+W` search, `Ctrl+G` help, `Alt+U` undo, `Ctrl+_` go to line number.

sections.title: vi / vim: modes
body: `vi` is installed on practically every Linux system, `vim` is its improved version (on some minimal systems `vi` is simply vim). Learn the basics once and you can fix a server in any situation.

The key idea: vim has **modes**. In **Normal mode** (default at start) keys are commands — typing `dd` deletes a line instead of writing text. With `i` you enter **Insert mode** and type normally; `Esc` takes you back. With `:` you enter **command-line mode** for `:w`, `:q`, `:wq`, `:q!`.
Beginner mistake number one: typing text while in Normal mode. If strange things happen, press `Esc` once or twice, then continue.

commands.what: Opens a file in vim (starts in Normal mode).
commands.where: For config files, scripts and on servers without nano.
commands.why: Available everywhere and very fast once learned.

commands.what: `i` enters Insert mode, `Esc` returns to Normal mode.
commands.where: Whenever you switch between typing and commanding.
commands.why: Without `i` you cannot type text; without `Esc` you cannot give commands.

commands.what: Writes the file and quits (also `ZZ` or `:x`).
commands.why: Saves and leaves in one step.

sections.danger: Stuck in vim? Press `Esc`, then type `:q!` and ENTER to quit WITHOUT saving, or `:wq` to save and quit. Ctrl+C or Ctrl+X do not exit vim.

sections.title: Essential vim commands
body: These Normal-mode commands cover most daily work. Arrow keys work, but `h j k l` (left, down, up, right) keep your hands on the home row.
Many commands take a number: `3dd` deletes three lines, `5j` moves five lines down. `gg` jumps to the top, `G` to the end, `:42` to line 42. Use `:set number` to show line numbers.

commands.what: Deletes (cuts) the current line; `p` pastes it below.
commands.why: Remove, move or duplicate lines (`yy` copies).

commands.what: Undoes the last change; `Ctrl+R` redoes it.
Searches forward for `text`; `n` jumps to the next match.
commands.why: Find settings in long config files.

commands.what: Quits and discards all unsaved changes.
commands.where: From Normal mode when you made a mess or just looked.
commands.why: The emergency exit; plain `:q` refuses if there are changes.

sections.tip: Run `vimtutor` once (about 30 minutes) — the best interactive vim course, installed with vim.

sections.title: Editing safely
body: System config files live in `/etc` and belong to root. As a normal user you can read them but not save changes: use `sudo nano /etc/file` only when you must. **Make a backup first** so you can restore after a typo.
Non-interactive alternatives need no editor: `echo "text" >> file` appends a line, `echo "text" > file` **overwrites** the whole file. With `cp file file.bak` you create a backup in one second.
If vim crashed or the terminal closed, a leftover swap file (`.file.swp`) may remain and vim warns on the next start. If nobody else is editing the file, you can delete the swap file.

commands.what: Creates a backup copy before editing.
commands.where: Before every change to an important file.
commands.why: You can restore the old state with `cp file.bak file`.

commands.what: Edits a root-owned file with your own editor via a temporary copy.
commands.why: Safer than running the whole editor as root.

commands.what: Sets the default editor used by tools such as `sudoedit` and `crontab -e`.
commands.why: Tools then open nano instead of an editor you do not know.

commands.what: Shows the file content without opening an editor.
commands.where: To verify the result of an edit.
commands.why: Quick check that the file contains what you expect.

sections.warn: Before editing a file under `/etc`, make a backup (`sudo cp file file.bak`). A broken `/etc/fstab` or `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` can make the machine unbootable or unreachable.
sections.tip: `>` overwrites, `>>` appends. One missing `>` can empty a file — check with `cat` afterwards.

t01.text: Create a file without an editor: `echo "hello editor" > hello.txt`.

t02.text: Show the content of the file with `cat hello.txt`.

t03.text: Back up `todo.txt` before editing it: `cp todo.txt todo.txt.bak`.
t03.hint: Source first, then the backup name.

t04.text: Append a line to `todo.txt` without an editor: `echo "buy bread" >> todo.txt`.

t05.text: Show `todo.txt` with line numbers using `cat -n todo.txt`.
t05.hint: In vim you would see them with `:set number`.

t06.text: Find the line with `report` and show its number: `grep -n report todo.txt`.
t06.hint: `-n` prints the line number in front.

t07.text: Predict: how many lines does `todo.txt` have now? Check with `wc -l todo.txt`.
t07.hint: It had 3 lines and you appended one.

t08.text: Predict: what happens when a normal user runs `echo test > /etc/motd`? Try it.
t08.hint: Expect Permission denied; editing system files needs sudo (and a backup).

t09.text: Debug: a bad edit broke `app.conf` (it says `mode=debug`). Restore the old version from `app.conf.bak`.
t09.hint: Copy the backup over the file with `cp`.

t10.text: Debug: vim keeps warning about a leftover swap file `.todo.txt.swp` in your home folder. Nobody is editing the file; delete the swap file.

t11.text: Mini project: create the folder `scripts`, write `scripts/hello.sh` containing the lines `#!/bin/bash` and `echo hello` (use `printf` with `\n`), then make it mode 755.

t12.text: Challenge: first back up `notes.txt` as `notes.txt.bak`, then append the line `meeting at 10` to `notes.txt`.
t12.hint: Order matters: `cp` before the edit, then `echo ... >>`.

t13.text: Challenge: from `server.log` save only the lines containing `ERROR` into `errors.txt`.
t13.hint: `grep` pattern file, with the output redirected using `>`.

t14.text: TICKET #2705 — New hires need a welcome note. Create `~/welcome.txt` containing `Welcome to linux-lab`, put a copy into `~/Documents/welcome.txt`, and make the copy read-only for everyone (mode 444).

q1.q: You are in vim and want to leave WITHOUT saving. What do you type?
q1.explain: `:q!` quits and discards changes; `:wq` would save them. Ctrl+X is nano's exit key, not vim's.

q2.q: In vim you type `dd` right after starting and a line disappears. Why?
options: dd is a typo in the file
You were in Normal mode where dd deletes a line
q2.explain: vim starts in Normal mode where keys are commands. `dd` deletes the current line; `u` undoes it.

options: Exits nano and asks to save changes
q3.explain: Ctrl+X exits; with unsaved changes nano asks Y/N. Ctrl+K cuts, Ctrl+G is help, Ctrl+W searches.

q4.q: What should you do before editing `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`?
options: Delete the file and create a new one
Run the editor as a normal user
Make a backup copy of it
Nothing, the file can be regenerated
q4.explain: A backup (`sudo cp file file.bak`) lets you restore quickly after an error.

summary: vim has modes: Normal (commands), Insert (`i`, text), command line (`:`). `Esc` returns to Normal.
Back up system files before editing; use `sudo` only when needed. `>` overwrites, `>>` appends.

glossary.meaning: vim's default mode in which keys are commands.
vim mode for typing text, entered with i, left with Esc.
A hidden .file.swp that vim creates while editing; it remains after a crash.
The in-memory copy of the file you edit until you save.
Environment variable naming the default editor for other tools.

vm.intro: On your VM you now use the real editors. Do all steps in your home directory with test files; take a snapshot before touching files in /etc.

v01.title: First file with nano
v01.text: Open nano, type the text, save with Ctrl+O and ENTER, exit with Ctrl+X. Then show the file.

blocks.cmd:
nano nano_test.txt
# type: hello nano   -> Ctrl+O, ENTER, Ctrl+X
cat nano_test.txt

differs: `command not found`: install nano with `sudo apt install nano` (Ubuntu) or `sudo dnf install nano` (Rocky/Alma).
If nano asks 'Save modified buffer?' on exit, press `Y` and ENTER.

v02.title: Cut and paste lines in nano
v02.text: In nano write `line one` and `line two`, save and exit. Reopen, cut the first line with Ctrl+K, paste it twice with Ctrl+U, save. Paste the result.

blocks.cmd:
nano lines.txt
# type two lines, save, exit
nano lines.txt
# Ctrl+K once, Ctrl+U twice, Ctrl+O, ENTER, Ctrl+X
cat -n lines.txt
blocks.expected:
1	line two
     2	line one
     3	line one

differs: If the order differs, it depends on where the cursor was when pasting; `line one` and `line two` must both appear.
No numbering shown? You forgot `-n` in `cat -n`.

v03.title: First file with vim
v03.text: Open vim, press `i`, type the text, then Esc and `:wq` ENTER. Show the file.

blocks.cmd:
vim vim_test.txt
# i  -> type: hello vim  -> Esc  -> :wq  -> ENTER
cat vim_test.txt

differs: Typed text is missing or odd? You did not press `i` first. Press Esc, `:q!`, and start again.
`vim: command not found`: use `vi vim_test.txt` or install vim (`sudo apt install vim` / `sudo dnf install vim-enhanced`).

v04.title: Quit without saving
v04.text: Write `keep` into a file, then open it in vim, add a line `lose` and leave with `:q!`. The file must still contain only `keep`.

blocks.cmd:
echo keep > discard.txt
vim discard.txt
# i -> type: lose -> Esc -> :q! -> ENTER
cat discard.txt

differs: If `lose` is in the file, you used `:wq` instead of `:q!`.
If vim refuses to quit with `:q`, that is the protection for unsaved changes: use `:q!`.

v05.title: Delete a line and undo
v05.text: Create a 20-line file, delete line 5 with `5G` then `dd`, press `u` to undo, then `dd` again and save. Count the lines.

blocks.cmd:
seq 1 20 > numbers.txt
vim numbers.txt
# 5G -> dd -> u -> dd -> :wq
wc -l numbers.txt

differs: Result 20: the final `dd` or the save did not happen; result 18: you deleted twice without `u`.
`seq` is missing? Use `for i in $(seq 1 20); do echo $i; done > numbers.txt` or install coreutils.

v06.title: Set the default editor
v06.text: Set nano as default editor for this session and check the variable.
differs: To make it permanent add `export EDITOR=nano` to `~/.bashrc`; it takes effect in a new shell.

v07.title: Backup before editing /etc
v07.text: Back up `/etc/hosts` with sudo, check the backup, and open the original with sudoedit or `sudo nano`. Look, change nothing, exit without saving.

blocks.cmd:
sudo cp /etc/hosts /etc/hosts.bak
ls -l /etc/hosts.bak
sudoedit /etc/hosts
# look around, then Ctrl+X (nano) or :q! (vim)

differs: `sudoedit` complains about the editor? Run `export EDITOR=nano` first, or use `sudo nano /etc/hosts`.
If `sudo` asks for a password, enter your own (nothing is displayed while typing).
